title: Do people apply different norms to humans and large language models acting on their behalf? Evidence from norm elicitations in two canonical economic games
abstract: arXiv:2601.15312v2 Announce Type: replace-cross  Abstract: While delegating tasks to large language models (LLMs) can save people time, there is growing evidence that offloading tasks to such models produces social costs. We elicit appropriateness of behavior in two canonical economic games to study whether people have different norms for humans and LLMs acting on their behalf. More specifically, we study the social appropriateness of a spectrum of possible behaviors: when LLMs divide resources on our behalf (Dictator Game and Ultimatum Game) and when they evaluate the fairness of resource splits (Ultimatum Game). We use the Krupka-Weber norm elicitation task to detect possible shifts in social appropriateness ratings. Results of two pre-registered and incentivized experimental studies using representative samples from the UK and US (N = 2,658) show three key findings. translated_title: 人们对人类和代表其行事的大语言模型是否适用不同的规范？来自两个经典经济博弈中的规范引出证据
translated_abstract: 虽然将任务委托给大语言模型（LLM）可以节省人们的时间，但越来越多的证据表明，将任务卸载给此类模型会产生社会成本。我们在两个经典经济博弈中引出行为的社会适当性评价，以研究人们对人类和代表其行事的LLM是否持有不同的规范。更具体地说，我们研究了一系列可能行为的社会适当性：当LLM代表我们分配资源时（独裁者博弈和最后通牒博弈），以及当它们评估资源分配的公平时（最后通牒博弈）。我们使用Krupka-Weber规范引出任务来检测社会适当性评分中可能出现的偏移。两项采用英国和美国代表性样本（N = 2,658）的预注册且有激励机制的实验研究结果显示出三个关键发现。首先，在独裁者博弈中，当独裁者是人类时，社会适当性最高的分配方式仍然是平均分配（原文在此处截断）。
tldr: 该研究通过在英美两国代表性样本（N=2,658）上开展的预注册激励实验，利用两个经典经济博弈发现人们对人类和代表其行事的大语言模型适用不同的社会规范。
en_tdlr: Using pre-registered, incentivized experiments with 2,658 representative participants from the UK and US across two canonical economic games, this study shows that people apply different social norms to humans versus large language models acting on their behalf.
